body_markdown:
***Gilat CEO Adi Sfadia shares his perspective on the evolving satellite communications landscape in the latest issue of the Asia Pacific Space Community Council’s quarterly newsletter, highlighting key industry trends – from network modernization and sovereign communications to the rising importance of resilient, adaptable SATCOM architectures that support government, defense, and future connectivity needs***


*Adi Sfadia serves as Gilat’s Chief Executive Officer, following five years as the company’s CFO. He has extensive financial leadership experience across public and private companies, including serving as CFO of communications and telecommunications companies Starhome Mach and RADVISION (Nasdaq: RVSN).*


***Q: Asia-Pacific is becoming an increasingly important region for emerging space initiatives. What are some of the most noteworthy trends happening in the region?***


A: Asia-Pacific is one of the world’s most dynamic satellite markets, reflecting a fundamental shift in mindset: satellite communications are now viewed as strategic national infrastructure, not merely a connectivity tool.


That shift is playing out in two connected ways. First, it is driving a more vibrant ecosystem across the value chain, as established operators and emerging players build capabilities that support national priorities and strengthen resilience during disruptions. India, Japan, and Korea are examples, with strong investment in satellite connectivity.


Second, that same recognition is pushing many countries toward sovereign satellite network capabilities, whether they are building them for the first time or expanding existing programs. At its core, this trend is about ownership and control: governments want to determine how their infrastructure is designed, operated, and secured rather than rely entirely on outside providers.


Sovereignty, however, is not only about satellites. It requires end-to-end control from the space segment to the ground segment and network operations, an area where Gilat brings deep expertise as a communications service integrator.


*The Gilat Defense Division is dedicated to meeting the specific needs of defense integrators, HLS, military, and government organizations worldwide. (Photo courtesy of Gilat Satellite Networks)*


***Q: A lot of attention in the media and industry is paid to a question about GEO, MEO and LEO, asking which will be the winning orbit. In your opinion, how should governments and operators across Asia-Pacific think about this issue?***


A: I believe the industry should be asking a different question. Rather than debating which orbit will “win,” governments, operators, and technology providers should be evaluating which architecture best meets their operational, commercial, and strategic objectives. The right answer depends on the specific use case, the performance requirements, and the assets already in place.


Our approach has always been to help customers build networks around their requirements, not around a particular orbital ideology. We focus on providing technologies and solutions that give operators the flexibility to meet operational objectives while remaining aligned with their financial and business models.


In Asia-Pacific, for example, countries that have invested in sovereign GEO satellite infrastructure are unlikely to abandon the unique capabilities those systems provide. GEO continues to play a critical role in supporting national resilience, sovereign communications, defense, public safety, and strategic economic development.


At the same time, LEO is creating significant new opportunities across consumer, enterprise and mobility markets, particularly where its capabilities align with customer requirements and economic considerations.


Ultimately, The objective should not be to replace one architecture with another, but to determine which approach, or combination of approaches, delivers the best outcome for a given mission or service.


In-flight connectivity is a good example. Airlines increasingly require both high performance and high availability, making it advantageous to leverage multiple orbital environments. Delivering that flexibility is often more important than advocating for one orbit over another.


A similar trend is emerging in government and defense communications, where resilience and assured connectivity are driving interest in multi-orbit architectures


At Gilat, our mission is to help customers maximize the value of their communications infrastructure, both today and in the future. We do that by leveraging our diverse technology portfolio to support evolving mission and market requirements while protecting existing investments and enabling the integration of new capabilities as they emerge.


***Q: What defense trends are having the greatest impact on satellite communications demand in Asia-Pacific?***


A: Three trends stand out.


First, defense organizations are placing greater emphasis on communications resilience. Rather than relying on any single network, technology, or point of failure, they are increasingly evaluating architectures that combine network diversity, automated failover, cyber resilience, and anti-jam capabilities to maintain communications in contested and degraded environments.


Second, relocatable and transportable ground infrastructure is becoming more important in modern defense communications. As military operations become more distributed, forces need capabilities that deploy rapidly, reposition as requirements evolve, and operate reliably across diverse environments.


Third, unmanned systems are taking on a larger role. As UAVs support more missions over greater distances, beyond-line-of-sight communications are becoming critical.


Together, these trends are shaping defense architectures designed for continuity, mobility, and flexibility.


*Gilat Satellite Networks’ was founded in 1987 and has customers in more than 100 countries, including across the APAC region.(Photo courtesy of Shutterstock)*


***Q: Asia-Pacific is one of the regions most exposed to natural disasters and large-scale disruptions. What role do you see satellite playing in improving preparedness and response?***


A: Satellite communications are essential to disaster preparedness and response across Asia-Pacific. When terrestrial networks are damaged or congested, satellite provides the resilient communications layer needed to maintain coordination and continuity.


But the priority is moving beyond connectivity. Governments and public safety organizations need solutions that help them gain situational awareness, coordinate resources, and make informed decisions during fast-moving events.


By integrating communications, data, monitoring systems, and operational workflows into a unified platform, organizations can enhance preparedness, coordination, and response. For homeland security agencies, this level of integration is increasingly critical. In regions frequently affected by earthquakes, typhoons, floods, wildfires, and other natural disasters, integrated solutions provide the situational awareness and operational coordination needed to improve response and accelerate community recovery.


***Q: Airlines across Asia-Pacific are expanding rapidly. How do you see in-flight connectivity evolving as part of this broader satellite story?***


A: Aviation is one of the clearest examples of how connectivity expectations continue to rise. Passengers expect the same experience in the air that they have on the ground, and airlines are under pressure to deliver it reliably across long-haul and regional routes alike.


Asia-Pacific presents a particular challenge because of its geographic scale, with aircraft often moving between orbital coverage zones.


As regional carriers grow and compete on passenger experience, I expect in-flight connectivity to become a differentiator, not just an amenity, with satellite central to making that possible. We are seeing growing demand for our Sidewinder ESA multi-orbit antenna and ground systems capabilities, including the ability to roam between networks.


***Q: Where do you see the most exciting opportunities for satellite communications beyond traditional connectivity services?***


A: Today, satellite connectivity is becoming integral to network architecture and critical infrastructure design. This marks a fundamental shift, positioning satellite as a strategic enabler of resilient, always-available communications. As a result, satellite now serves as a key differentiator across defense and commercial applications, where operational continuity and network resilience are essential.


Value is also created as satellite connectivity becomes integrated with cloud platforms, evolves toward 5G NTN, and connects with AI-driven analytics, IoT devices, enterprise applications, and operational systems. In that environment, connectivity becomes an enabler, not the end objective.


This opens the door to new business models and use cases. The question is no longer, “How do I connect a remote location?” but “How do I improve an operational outcome?” Whether the goal is efficiency, automation, or real-time decision-making, communications are one component of a broader solution.


I believe this evolution will reshape the satellite industry. Success will be defined less by bandwidth delivered and more by the value created through the applications, services, and outcomes that connectivity enables.
